L01-C01.title: L01-C01 · Three routes reach the same destination: P has road times 4 + 4, Q has 1 + 2 + 2, and R has 6 + 1 minutes. Which comparison of road count and total time is correct?
choices: P and R tie for fewest roads; Q is fastest at 5 minutes.
P and R tie for fewest roads; R is fastest at 1 minute.
Q uses the fewest roads and is fastest at 5 minutes.
P and R tie for fewest roads and must tie for fastest time.

L01-C02.title: L01-C02 · A search removes the oldest waiting path and adds children at the back. Its queue is [B, C, D], next first. B is expanded, adding E then F; C is then expanded, adding H. No node is a goal. Which two nodes are selected next?
choices: D, then E.
E, then F.
H, then D.
D, then H.

L01-C03.title: L01-C03 · A search removes the most recently added path. It pushes B, then C, then D onto an empty stack. After selecting D, it pushes J, then K. J and K have no children; K is then selected. No node is a goal. Which two nodes are selected next?
choices: C, then B.
C, then J.
J, then B.
J, then C.

L01-C04.title: L01-C04 · In a finite tree, the only goals are G at depth 3 with path cost 12, and H at depth 4 with path cost 4. All edge costs are positive. Iterative deepening increases its limit from 0 by one each time and stops at its first goal. What does it return, and why?
choices: H: positive edge costs make the deeper goal cheaper to find.
H: iterative deepening compares total costs across all limits.
G: the depth-3 pass reaches it before H is allowed; fewest edges need not mean lowest cost.
G: the first goal found must have minimum cost whenever all edge costs are positive.

L01-C05.title: L01-C05 · Only these directed edges exist: S→G costs 9, S→A costs 2, A→G costs 8, S→B costs 4, and B→G costs 1. After expanding S, a search selects the waiting path with the lowest cost so far. Which path comes next, and which complete route is cheapest?
choices: Next S→G; cheapest S→G, because a goal has already been discovered.
Next S→B; cheapest S→B→G, because its final edge is cheapest.
Next S→A; cheapest S→B→G, with total cost 5.
Next S→A; cheapest S→A→G, because A is selected first.

L01-C06.title: L01-C06 · The frontier contains paths P, Q and R. Their costs so far g and remaining estimates h are: P (6, 1), Q (2, 4), R (4, 3). Greedy selects minimum h; A* selects minimum g + h. Which paths do they select next?
choices: Both select P, because its remaining estimate is smallest.
Both select Q, because its cost so far is smallest.
Greedy selects P; A* selects Q, whose total estimate is 6.
Greedy selects P; A* ties P and R at a total estimate of 7.

L01-C07.title: L01-C07 · Graph A* has expanded X at cost g = 6 and found X→G with cost 3. Later it finds a route to X at g = 4. Its heuristic is admissible but inconsistent; G is the goal. Which action preserves the cheaper route through X?
choices: Keep X closed: an admissible heuristic makes its first expansion final.
Update X to g = 4, but do not revisit its outgoing edge; keep G at cost 9.
Reopen X at g = 4, but keep G at cost 9 because a goal was already discovered.
Update X’s cost and parent, reopen it, and propagate the improvement to G at cost 7.

L01-C08.title: L01-C08 · Branch-and-bound already holds a complete route costing 6. Waiting path P has g = 4, h = 3; Q has g = 2, h = 4. The estimates are admissible and costs nonnegative. If the aim is to return one cheapest route, which paths may be pruned?
choices: Only P: a lower bound equal to 6 must always be explored.
Only Q: its remaining estimate is larger than P’s.
Both P and Q: neither lower bound is below 6, and the saved route is retained.
Neither: their costs so far are below 6, so both must be completed.

L01-C09.title: L01-C09 · A graph A* search uses an admissible but inconsistent heuristic and never reopens expanded states. Can its first selected goal be suboptimal? Explain using the reopening example, where cost 6 improves to 5, and state the repair.

L01-O01.title: L01-O01 · A robot moves horizontally or vertically on a grid, one unit per move, and must avoid obstacles. Which proposed heuristic is guaranteed admissible for every reachable state?
choices: The length of any legal route already found from that state to the goal.
Manhattan distance plus 1, to compensate for possible obstacles.
Twice Manhattan distance when the map contains many obstacles.
Manhattan distance to the goal with the obstacles ignored.

L01-O02.title: L01-O02 · The only directed edges are S→A, S→B, A→X and B→X. A search rejects a child only if its state already appears on that same path; it has no global visited set. What happens to S→A→X and S→B→X?
choices: The second path is rejected as a cycle because X was reached on the first path.
Both paths are rejected because a state may have only one parent.
Both paths are kept: neither contains a cycle, though both end at X.
The second path is automatically merged with the first by the path cycle check.

L01-O03.title: L01-O03 · An edge u→v costs 2. The heuristic values are h(u) = 5 and h(v) = 2; the current path to u has cost g = 3. After extending that path to v, how does its A* score f = g + h change, and is this edge consistent?
choices: f rises from 8 to 9; the edge is consistent because the step costs 2.
f falls from 8 to 7; the edge is consistent because its cost is positive.
f stays at 8; the increase in g always exactly cancels the change in h.
f falls from 8 to 7; the edge is inconsistent because 5 > 2 + 2.
